title: 1 Chronicles 9:1–16
context: Verse 1 closes the genealogies of “all Israel” and states plainly that Judah was carried away to Babylon “for their disobedience.” The list that follows names the first inhabitants who lived again in their cities, beginning with Jerusalem’s residents from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, and then priests and Levites. Many names and figures parallel Nehemiah 11:3–19, with some differences in names and numbers (for example, 956 Benjamites in 9:9 and 928 in Nehemiah 11:8), and Nehemiah 11:4 mentions only Judah and Benjamin among Jerusalem’s residents, where 9:3 adds Ephraim and Manasseh. The text does not explain the differences, and this page does not harmonize them. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: exile was just judgment, yet God brought his people back and restored the worship of his house.

verses.text: So all Israel were listed by genealogies; and behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel. Judah was carried away captive to Babylon for their disobedience.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel is listed by genealogies, and Judah was carried away to Babylon “for their disobedience.” Arminian readers stress that the exile was the just result of the people’s persistent and responsible unfaithfulness, after many warnings and opportunities to repent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that the exile was God’s righteous judgment on real sin, and they see God’s purpose to preserve a people continuing through it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a plain confession that the exile was deserved, and that the genealogies testify to God’s faithfulness beyond it.

verses.text: Now the first inhabitants who lived in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.
verses.arminianNotes: The first inhabitants to live again in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants. Arminian readers note that the returned community took up its responsibilities in the land, each group with its own role in restored life and worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in bringing his people back as he promised. The list parallels Nehemiah 11:3. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the beginning of restoration, with the people, priests, and Levites together resuming the life God had given them.

verses.text: In Jerusalem, there lived of the children of Judah, of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim and Manasseh:
verses.arminianNotes: In Jerusalem lived people from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Arminian readers note that the list includes northern tribes as well as Judah and Benjamin, which reflects the Chronicler’s concern for “all Israel” (9:1). Nehemiah 11:4 names only Judah and Benjamin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the inclusion of Ephraim and Manasseh and the Chronicler’s vision of a united people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an expression of hope that all Israel belongs in the restored community, and they note the difference from Nehemiah 11:4 without harmonizing.

verses.text: Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Perez the son of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Uthai of the line of Perez son of Judah heads the list of Judah’s residents. Arminian readers note that Perez is the ancestor of David’s line (2:4–15). The returned community traced its roots carefully, honoring the families from which it came.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the link to Perez and the royal line of David, a reminder of God’s promises to David even after the exile. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting the restored community with its history and with the line through which God’s purposes ran.

verses.text: Of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn and his sons.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the Shilonites, Asaiah the firstborn and his sons are named. Arminian readers note that the Shilonites appear to be a family of Judah, though the exact connection is not explained. The record keeps each family’s place among the returned residents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the uncertainty and read the verse as part of a careful list of returned families. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical record and see in it the reestablishment of Judah’s households in Jerusalem.

verses.text: Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their brothers, six hundred ninety.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Zerah, Jeuel and their brothers number 690. Arminian readers note that the record includes the descendants of Zerah, Perez’s brother (2:4), alongside those of Perez. Both branches of Judah had a place in the restored city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the inclusion of Zerah’s line and the completeness of the record. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence of a broad return from Judah and affirm that God gathered families from many branches of his people.

verses.text: Of the sons of Benjamin: Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hassenuah;
verses.arminianNotes: Of Benjamin, Sallu son of Meshullam is named with his ancestry. Arminian readers note that Nehemiah 11:7 also names Sallu son of Meshullam, though with a different line of ancestors. The record preserves the identity of Benjamite families in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the parallel and its differences, and they do not force a harmony. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the list of returned residents and see in Benjamin’s presence the restoration of the tribe that had stood with Judah.

verses.text: and Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri; and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah;
verses.arminianNotes: Ibneiah, Elah, and Meshullam are named with their fathers. Arminian readers note the careful record of ancestry, which mattered for identity in the restored community. Each family could show its place among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the importance of genealogical records for a people rebuilding after exile. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the list of Benjamite residents and affirm that God restored real families to their homes.

verses.text: and their brothers, according to their generations, nine hundred fifty-six. All these men were heads of fathers’ households by their fathers’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: Their brothers number 956, all heads of fathers’ households. Arminian readers note that Nehemiah 11:8 gives 928 for Benjamin, a difference recorded in the context without harmonizing. The point is the substantial return of Benjamite families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difference in numbers and focus on the reality of the return. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as testimony to God’s faithfulness in restoring Benjamin and decline to build doctrine on the figures.

verses.text: Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin,
verses.arminianNotes: Of the priests, Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin are named. Arminian readers note that priestly families resumed their service in Jerusalem. Worship was not left to chance; specific families took up their responsibility before God and the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jehoiarib and Jedaiah receive the first and second priestly courses (24:7) and Jachin the twenty-first (24:17), and that Nehemiah 11:10 gives a similar list. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the restoration of priestly service, central to the community’s life with God.

verses.text: and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of God’s house;
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah son of Hilkiah, of Zadok’s line, is “the ruler of God’s house.” Arminian readers note the continuity of the priestly line through Zadok. Faithful leadership in worship is honored as a vital part of the restored community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Zadokite line as a sign of God’s faithfulness to the priesthood. Nehemiah 11:11 names Seraiah at this point, with the same ancestors, a difference stated plainly here. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring the leadership of God’s house.

verses.text: and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashhur, the son of Malchijah; and Maasai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;
verses.arminianNotes: Adaiah and Maasai are named with long lines of ancestors. Arminian readers note the care taken to establish priestly credentials. Those who served in God’s house needed to show that they belonged to the priestly families, and the record supplies that proof.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the importance of a proven lineage for priestly service. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the restored priesthood’s record and see in it the community’s concern to worship God according to his appointed order.

verses.text: and their brothers, heads of their fathers’ houses, one thousand seven hundred sixty; they were very able men for the work of the service of God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Their brothers, heads of houses, number 1,760, “very able men for the work of the service of God’s house.” Arminian readers note the commendation of their ability and diligence. Service in God’s house called for skill, commitment, and readiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the large number of priests and their fitness for service. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring those who devoted themselves to worship and affirm that the restoration of God’s house required many faithful workers.

verses.text: Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;
verses.arminianNotes: Of the Levites, Shemaiah of the sons of Merari is named. Arminian readers note that the Levites resumed their distinct roles alongside the priests. The record shows the restored community ordering its worship according to the patterns God had given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the Levitical line and the parallel in Nehemiah 11:15. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the restoration of Levitical service and see in it the community’s faithful return to ordered worship.

verses.text: and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Mica, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph,
verses.arminianNotes: Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, and Mattaniah of the line of Asaph are named. Arminian readers note that Asaph’s descendants led worship through music. The return of these families meant the return of praise to Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Asaph’s line and its link to David’s ordering of worship (6:39). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence that the restored community resumed the service of song, honoring God with the music established in David’s day.

verses.text: and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun; and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.
verses.arminianNotes: Obadiah of Jeduthun’s line and Berechiah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites, are named. Arminian readers note that some Levites lived outside Jerusalem, coming in to serve. The arrangement reflects practical responsibility in a growing community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Jeduthun’s line and the Levites’ residence in nearby villages. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the record of restored worship and see in it the community’s careful provision for the service of God’s house.
